title: Annual Research Review: Infant Development, Autism, and ADHD—Early Pathways to Emerging Disorders

subsections.section_title: Conceptual and Epidemiological Foundations of Early Neurodevelopmental Pathways
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual and Epidemiological Foundations of Early Neurodevelopmental Pathways - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are best understood as early-emerging neurodevelopmental conditions whose clinical presentation reflects both developmental timing and population-level heterogeneity. Epidemiological work on ASD has shown substantial variation in reported prevalence across settings, attributable not only to true population differences but also to changes in case definition, ascertainment, and service systems, underscoring that prevalence estimates are inseparable from diagnostic context ref [1]. This is especially important in infancy-focused research, where the goal is not merely earlier detection of fixed categories, but identification of developmental pathways that may culminate in different outcomes.

A developmental perspective is further warranted because diagnosis is often delayed relative to the onset of atypical behavior. Reviews of age at ASD diagnosis indicate that family, clinician, and system-level factors all shape when children are identified, while work on diagnosis in 2- and 3-year-olds shows that reliable classification is possible in many cases but remains constrained by symptom stability and developmental change ref [14], ref [25]. At the same time, multisite evidence demonstrates that diagnostic distinctions within the autism spectrum have historically shown inconsistency across clinical settings, reinforcing the need to treat early phenotypes as evolving rather than static entities ref [21]. Evidence-based assessment frameworks similarly emphasize integrating behavioral observation, developmental history, and standardized measures when characterizing early risk ref [33].

For conceptualizing early pathways, it is also critical to recognize overlap between ASD and ADHD. High rates of co-occurrence, alongside evidence for shared heritability and partially overlapping cognitive and neural endophenotypes, suggest that these conditions cannot be fully understood in isolation ref [31], ref [17], ref [29]. Accordingly, infancy provides a key window for examining both shared liability and disorder-specific divergence, laying the foundation for later sections on emerging mechanisms and trajectories.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual and Epidemiological Foundations of Early Neurodevelopmental Pathways
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual and Epidemiological Foundations of Early Neurodevelopmental Pathways - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central conceptual shift in early neurodevelopmental research has been from viewing autism and ADHD as fixed diagnostic categories toward understanding them as heterogeneous, developmentally unfolding spectra of variation. Within autism in particular, spectrum models emphasize marked diversity in symptom expression, developmental timing, and associated cognitive profiles, encouraging questions about how early infancy pathways may diverge before later clinical syndromes become apparent ref [14], ref [6]. This perspective is especially important in infancy, when behavioral signs may be subtle, uneven across domains, and not yet organized into the syndromic patterns captured by later diagnostic criteria.

At the same time, a developmental framework must accommodate both disorder-specific liabilities and trans-diagnostic processes. Reviews of autism heterogeneity have argued that constraining broad phenotypic variation requires attention to specific developmental systems, such as social brain circuitry, and to how perturbations in these systems interact over time ref [6]. In parallel, work on reaction time variability highlights one candidate trans-diagnostic phenotype spanning ADHD and ASD, suggesting that some early pathways may reflect shared alterations in attention regulation, arousal, or information processing rather than wholly distinct disorder boundaries ref [24]. Such constructs help bridge categorical diagnoses with dimensional models of risk.

Epidemiologically, these conceptual developments matter because population prevalence and case identification depend heavily on where thresholds are drawn within continuously distributed traits. The autism spectrum framework underscores that broadening diagnostic definitions can increase ascertainment of milder or atypical presentations ref [14], while trans-diagnostic phenotypes may illuminate why co-occurring or overlapping features are common across neurodevelopmental conditions ref [24]. Together, these perspectives justify studying infancy not simply as a prediagnostic phase for separate disorders, but as a period in which shared and distinct developmental trajectories are progressively differentiated ref [6], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual and Epidemiological Foundations of Early Neurodevelopmental Pathways
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual and Epidemiological Foundations of Early Neurodevelopmental Pathways - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central conceptual issue in early neurodevelopmental research is how diagnostic boundaries shape epidemiological estimates and developmental inference. Changes from DSM-IV pervasive developmental disorder categories to the broader DSM-5 autism spectrum construct can alter who is counted as a case, with direct implications for prevalence estimates, sample composition, and interpretation of longitudinal risk markers ref [20]. These shifts reinforce the need to view early traits dimensionally, especially in infancy when symptom profiles are incomplete and heterogeneity is pronounced.

Measurement challenges are particularly salient in the first years of life. Screening and diagnostic instruments for autism have improved case identification, but their performance depends on developmental level, informant report, and the distinction between surveillance, screening, and formal diagnosis ref [16]. Prospective infant-sibling work illustrates this point: behavioral features detectable at 18 months can predict later outcomes, yet prediction is probabilistic rather than deterministic, with different combinations of social-communicative, cognitive, and motor indicators mapping onto later ASD-related trajectories ref [18].

This dimensional perspective is further supported by studies of candidate endophenotypes and cross-domain phenotypes. Developmental differences in resting EEG power have been proposed as one marker of altered neural maturation associated with ASD liability ref [12], while sensory-based subgrouping highlights meaningful within-diagnosis variation that may cut across conventional behavioral categories ref [29]. At the same time, overlap with ADHD-related traits is epidemiologically and conceptually important: ADHD symptoms covary with autism behavioral severity in some samples ref [19], and differences in sensory-motor learning profiles across ADHD and autism suggest both shared neurodevelopmental vulnerability and disorder-specific processing biases ref [31]. Together, these findings justify studying early pathways as partially shared, probabilistic, and developmentally dynamic rather than as fixed disorder categories.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual and Epidemiological Foundations of Early Neurodevelopmental Pathways
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual and Epidemiological Foundations of Early Neurodevelopmental Pathways - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central conceptual issue in early neurodevelopment is how to reconcile categorical diagnoses with evidence for distributed familial liability. Work on the broader autism phenotype indicates that subclinical social-communicative, linguistic, and rigid-behavioral characteristics are detectable in relatives, supporting the view that autistic traits are continuously distributed rather than confined to diagnostic boundaries ref [19]. This perspective is especially relevant in infancy, where mild or partial expressions of liability may precede later categorical outcomes and complicate simple case-control distinctions.

At the same time, early pathways are markedly heterogeneous. Studies of toddlers with autism spectrum disorder have identified multiple developmental trajectories rather than a single uniform course, with variation in symptom onset, rate of change, and domains of impairment ref [25]. Such findings strengthen the epidemiological rationale for prospective infant studies: early atypicality should be understood as a set of probabilistic pathways, some leading to persistent ASD, others to broader neurodevelopmental difficulties, and others to more subtle phenotypic expressions.

This heterogeneity also underpins the growing emphasis on very early identification and intervention in infants at elevated familial risk. The case for intervention before full syndrome consolidation rests on developmental plasticity and on the possibility that emerging social-attentional differences may alter subsequent learning cascades ref [31]. Consistent with this developmental-probabilistic model, autism severity appears to reflect the combined average contribution of de novo and familial influences, linking population variation in symptom burden to multiple etiological routes rather than a unitary cause ref [34]. Together, these observations provide a framework for studying shared and distinct pathways to ASD and ADHD from the first year of life.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual and Epidemiological Foundations of Early Neurodevelopmental Pathways
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual and Epidemiological Foundations of Early Neurodevelopmental Pathways - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A key epidemiological implication for early neurodevelopmental models is that ASD and ADHD should not be treated as wholly separate pathways. Reviews of their relationship consistently show substantial phenotypic overlap, shared impairments in attention and self-regulation, and high rates of co-occurrence, indicating that early liability may be partly transdiagnostic rather than disorder-specific ref [9], ref [28]. This perspective is important in infancy, where emerging symptoms are often diffuse and may later crystallize into ASD, ADHD, or combined presentations.

Population and service-based studies further show that case identification is shaped by screening practices and diagnostic systems. Systematic pediatric screening initiatives and general-population studies demonstrate that ASD-related features can be detected as early as 18 months, although sensitivity and specificity depend on follow-up and developmental change ref [18], ref [27]. At the same time, preschool diagnostic data from community settings indicate that ascertainment in real-world populations reflects both symptom expression and local service organization, reinforcing the need to interpret prevalence and age-at-diagnosis estimates developmentally ref [24].

Familial and clinical data also support a pathway model that integrates shared risk with later differentiation. Parental psychiatric history is associated with ASD risk, suggesting that early developmental vulnerability is embedded in broader familial psychopathology rather than isolated to a single syndrome ref [20]. Clinically, the frequent need to manage co-occurring ADHD and ASD underscores that comorbidity is not an exception but a common developmental outcome with consequences for assessment and treatment planning ref [12]. Together, these findings strengthen the rationale for studying early infancy as the period in which shared liabilities and disorder-specific trajectories begin to diverge ref [9], ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Genetic, Familial, and Neurobiological Mechanisms in ASD and ADHD Risk
subsections.subsection_title: Genetic, Familial, and Neurobiological Mechanisms in ASD and ADHD Risk - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A useful starting point for mechanistic accounts of early vulnerability is that ASD and ADHD are both strongly familial and highly heritable, but they are not etiologically independent. Genetic evidence indicates partial overlap in liability across the two conditions, supporting models in which some infants inherit transdiagnostic risk that may later differentiate into ASD, ADHD, or combined phenotypes depending on developmental timing and interacting influences ref [17]. At the same time, genetics reviews of ASD emphasize marked heterogeneity, including contributions from rare and common variants and complex polygenic architectures, implying that early pathways are unlikely to be unitary even within a single diagnostic category ref [18].

This partial sharing of liability is consistent with findings on co-occurrence in childhood, where ASD and ADHD frequently present together at rates higher than expected by chance. Reviews of comorbidity argue that overlap is not merely a diagnostic artifact, but likely reflects shared familial and neurodevelopmental mechanisms alongside disorder-specific influences ref [31]. Endophenotype models further suggest that cognitive and brain-based traits such as attentional control, executive dysfunction, and atypical information processing may index pleiotropic genetic effects that precede full clinical syndromes and help explain both overlap and divergence between ASD and ADHD outcomes ref [29].

From a developmental neurobiology perspective, early-emerging alterations in neural systems may be one route through which genetic liability becomes behaviorally expressed. Accounts of ASD neurobiology emphasize atypical trajectories of brain development rather than static lesions, highlighting the importance of timing, circuit specialization, and cascading effects on social and attentional functions ref [26]. Although genetic liability is central, prenatal and perinatal exposures may also modulate risk expression; reviews of maternal lifestyle and environmental factors in ASD suggest that non-genetic influences should be considered as contributors that may interact with inherited susceptibility during infancy ref [34].

subsections.section_title: Genetic, Familial, and Neurobiological Mechanisms in ASD and ADHD Risk
subsections.subsection_title: Genetic, Familial, and Neurobiological Mechanisms in ASD and ADHD Risk - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A complementary mechanistic account of early ASD/ADHD liability focuses on neurobiological endophenotypes that may channel genetic and familial risk into divergent developmental trajectories. In ASD, work on the developing social brain argues that heterogeneity can be constrained by examining how early-emerging neural systems for social orienting, face processing, and social attention become progressively specialized; disruption in these systems may provide a pathway from broad liability to disorder-specific social-communicative impairment rather than a unitary global deficit ref [6]. This framework is particularly relevant in infancy because it links familial risk to alterations in experience-dependent brain development.

Neuroanatomical findings further suggest that some infant biomarkers may be relatively specific to ASD risk. Early brain enlargement and elevated extra-axial cerebrospinal fluid have been reported in infants who later develop ASD, implying that atypical brain growth and fluid regulation may index prodromal neurodevelopmental divergence before full behavioral syndrome expression ref [8]. At the other end of development, large-scale MRI evidence in adults indicates that anatomical variation in ASD remains distributed and behaviorally relevant, reinforcing the view that brain-based liability is heterogeneous but measurable across the lifespan ref [27]. Biochemical work also points to partially distinct mechanisms, with meta-analytic evidence for altered blood serotonin levels in ASD supporting serotonergic dysregulation as one candidate pathway linking molecular risk to neural development ref [10].

By contrast, cross-disorder markers may illuminate shared liability. Reaction time variability has been proposed as a trans-diagnostic phenotype spanning ADHD and ASD, potentially reflecting common inefficiencies in arousal regulation, attentional control, or performance monitoring systems ref [24]. Taken together, the literature supports a layered model in which some neurobiological signatures appear more closely tied to ASD-specific developmental mechanisms, whereas others index broader liabilities that may contribute to ADHD, ASD, or combined phenotypes depending on how they interact with early brain maturation and environmental input ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Genetic, Familial, and Neurobiological Mechanisms in ASD and ADHD Risk
subsections.subsection_title: Genetic, Familial, and Neurobiological Mechanisms in ASD and ADHD Risk - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A useful mechanistic bridge between familial liability and infant phenotype is the concept of endophenotypes—measurable biological characteristics that index inherited risk before full disorder expression. In ASD, longitudinal work on resting EEG suggests that atypical developmental trajectories of neural oscillatory power may function as such an endophenotype, differentiating high-risk infants prior to stable diagnosis and pointing to altered cortical maturation as an early pathway from genetic liability to behavior ref [12]. Broader biomarker frameworks similarly emphasize that molecular, electrophysiological, and sensory-motor markers are unlikely to map cleanly onto diagnostic categories, but may instead capture partially shared neurodevelopmental liabilities relevant to both ASD and ADHD ref [28].

At the molecular level, candidate-gene and signaling accounts underscore the heterogeneity of ASD risk. Evidence implicating OXTR polymorphisms and plasma oxytocin concentrations links variation in social neuropeptide systems to dimensional social impairment across children with and without ASD, supporting a liability model in which genetic effects may influence social functioning continuously rather than categorically ref [39]. Likewise, support for ENGRAILED 2 as a susceptibility locus points to early transcriptional control of brain development as one route to ASD vulnerability ref [24]. More broadly, synaptic models propose that diverse genetic risks may converge on excitatory-inhibitory balance, synapse formation, and plasticity, offering a biologically plausible explanation for why distinct genetic variants can produce overlapping developmental outcomes ref [14].

These mechanistic accounts align with infant-sibling findings showing that early behavioral markers at 18 months predict later ASD-related outcomes, implying that familial risk is expressed through evolving neurocognitive and regulatory systems rather than a single fixed deficit ref [18]. Cross-disorder comparisons in sensorimotor learning further suggest both overlap and specificity: ADHD appears to rely on integrated sensory inputs during motor learning, whereas autism shows over-selective dependence on proprioceptive information, indicating that atypical sensory weighting may represent one neurobiological pathway by which shared developmental liability becomes phenotypically differentiated ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Genetic, Familial, and Neurobiological Mechanisms in ASD and ADHD Risk
subsections.subsection_title: Genetic, Familial, and Neurobiological Mechanisms in ASD and ADHD Risk - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A useful mechanistic bridge between familial liability and infant developmental divergence comes from work on intermediate phenotypes. The broader autism phenotype indicates that subclinical social-communicative rigidity, language style, and personality traits aggregate in relatives, supporting the view that inherited liability is distributed dimensionally rather than confined to categorical diagnosis ref [19]. Consistent with this, autism severity appears to reflect the combined influence of de novo events and familial transmission, implying that early pathways may differ across infants as a function of the relative weight of rare and inherited risk sources ref [34].

At the molecular level, candidate susceptibility genes such as CNTNAP2 have been especially informative because they link genetic variation to language, social behavior, and neural connectivity, offering a plausible route from inherited liability to early-emerging neurodevelopmental atypicality ref [6]. Such findings are most useful when interpreted probabilistically: they do not specify a single ASD pathway, but instead suggest that some infants may begin life with altered constraints on circuit formation that increase susceptibility to later ASD features or mixed ASD-ADHD phenotypes.

Neurobiological evidence further supports this multi-level account. Structural MRI studies in ASD have identified atypical patterns of brain anatomy and developmental organization, consistent with the idea that risk is expressed through altered trajectories of neural systems maturation rather than a static lesion model ref [20]. In parallel, evidence for disturbed cingulate glutamate metabolism lends support to excitatory/inhibitory imbalance models, which may help explain how genetic liability translates into altered information processing and behavioral inflexibility ref [33]. Together, familial aggregation, susceptibility genes, and neural systems findings support a developmental framework in which both inherited and biologically proximal mechanisms shape early vulnerability to ASD, with likely implications for overlap and divergence from ADHD pathways ref [19], ref [34].

subsections.section_title: Genetic, Familial, and Neurobiological Mechanisms in ASD and ADHD Risk
subsections.subsection_title: Genetic, Familial, and Neurobiological Mechanisms in ASD and ADHD Risk - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A useful synthesis of early vulnerability is to view ASD and ADHD risk as arising from partially overlapping liability systems that include inherited susceptibility, familial psychiatric loading, and perturbations to early neuroimmune development. Family aggregation data indicate that parental psychiatric disorders are associated with elevated likelihood of ASD in offspring, supporting the idea that broad, cross-diagnostic familial liability contributes to atypical developmental trajectories rather than mapping neatly onto a single categorical outcome ref [20]. Consistent with this, reviews of ASD–ADHD overlap emphasize that comorbidity is common and likely reflects both shared and disorder-specific etiological influences operating from early in development ref [9], ref [28].

At the molecular level, candidate genetic and pathway-based approaches suggest that risk may be distributed across interacting biological systems rather than isolated genes. Gene pathway analyses have been proposed as one route to improving prediction of ASD diagnosis, highlighting the relevance of convergent biological networks ref [27]. Immune-related mechanisms are also implicated: HLA transmission findings point to possible involvement of immune-genetic variation in ASD susceptibility ref [17], while maternal immune activation models identify interleukin-6 signaling as a plausible mechanistic pathway through which prenatal inflammatory exposure could alter fetal brain development and later social-communicative outcome ref [46].

For infant research, the mechanistic challenge is to link these distal liabilities to early-emerging phenotypes. One example is atypical cry acoustics at 6 months in infants at familial risk for ASD, which may index early alterations in arousal, sensorimotor control, or brainstem-limbic regulation before full behavioral syndromes are apparent ref [14]. Such markers are unlikely to be disorder-pure; rather, they may reflect shared developmental perturbations that, in interaction with genetic background and family psychiatric history, channel infants toward ASD, ADHD, or combined phenotypes ref [9], ref [20].

subsections.section_title: Early Behavioral and Cognitive Markers in Infancy
subsections.subsection_title: Early Behavioral and Cognitive Markers in Infancy - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A useful starting point for identifying infant markers is the growing view that ASD and ADHD are not wholly discrete developmental pathways, but partially overlapping neurodevelopmental liabilities. Genetic overlap and pleiotropic models suggest that early differences in attention control, arousal regulation, and information processing may index shared risk, even when later phenotypes diverge toward predominantly autistic or ADHD-like presentations ref [17], ref [29]. This perspective is reinforced by evidence that co-occurrence between the conditions is common and clinically meaningful, implying that infant markers should be interpreted dimensionally rather than as disorder-specific signals ref [31].

Within this framework, early behavioral variation in social orienting and attentional engagement is especially informative. Developmental accounts of ASD emphasize that atypicalities in how infants allocate attention to social and nonsocial input may emerge before the full syndrome is behaviorally apparent, reflecting altered trajectories in experience-dependent brain development ref [26]. At the same time, models spanning ASD and ADHD highlight candidate endophenotypes in attentional selection and executive control that may precede later diagnostic differentiation ref [29]. Thus, reduced social attention, atypical disengagement, or heightened distractibility in infancy may be better understood as early markers of neurodevelopmental divergence than as highly specific predictors of one condition alone ref [26], ref [31].

This has practical implications for prospective infant research. Because reliable categorical diagnosis is typically deferred until the toddler period, infant studies should prioritize repeated measurement of dimensional behaviors that feed into later diagnostic formulations ref [25]. Such an approach is consistent with developmental neurobiology accounts of ASD and with transdiagnostic formulations of ASD-ADHD overlap, both of which argue that early-emerging behavioral markers reflect interacting liabilities whose clinical expression becomes clearer over time ref [25], ref [26], ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Early Behavioral and Cognitive Markers in Infancy
subsections.subsection_title: Early Behavioral and Cognitive Markers in Infancy - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central line of work on early markers concerns how infants allocate attention to socially relevant information. Models of autism development emphasize that perturbations in the social brain may alter the emergence of social orienting and reciprocity from the first year of life, with cascading effects on later communication and learning ref [6]. Eye-tracking research has been especially important here because it can quantify subtle differences in gaze allocation before overt symptoms are clinically obvious, including reduced attention to faces, eyes, or biological motion and atypical patterns of visual exploration across social scenes ref [12].

These early attentional signatures should not be interpreted as unitary or autism-specific in a simple sense. Cross-disorder work suggests that variability in attentional control and response consistency may represent a broader neurocognitive liability relevant to both ASD and ADHD, even if the behavioral expression differs by developmental pathway ref [24]. In infancy, therefore, atypical looking patterns may reflect not only reduced social preference but also emerging difficulties in sustaining attention, filtering competing input, or regulating moment-to-moment engagement.

Behavioral markers also extend beyond social attention. Early repetitive or restricted patterns of object exploration and behavior, although more robustly characterized in toddlerhood, are important because they may signal developmental canalization toward later ASD phenotypes ref [32]. At the same time, neurodevelopmental studies indicate that altered brain growth trajectories, including early enlargement and elevated extra-axial fluid in infants later diagnosed with ASD, may accompany or precede these behavioral differences ref [8]. Taken together, early social-orienting atypicalities, attentional instability, and emerging repetitive behavior are best viewed as interacting markers that help differentiate developmental trajectories rather than as isolated predictors.

subsections.section_title: Early Behavioral and Cognitive Markers in Infancy
subsections.subsection_title: Early Behavioral and Cognitive Markers in Infancy - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Sensory processing and early sensorimotor organization are increasingly viewed as candidate markers of diverging developmental pathways in infants at elevated likelihood for ASD and, potentially, ADHD. Work on sensory-based phenotypes in ASD suggests that atypical responsivity is not unitary but clusters into distinguishable subtypes, implying that early sensory features may help parse heterogeneity rather than simply index overall symptom burden ref [29]. Converging neurophysiological evidence from developmental trajectories of resting EEG power further supports the idea that early differences in basic neural signaling may function as endophenotypic indicators of later ASD-related outcomes ref [12].

Behaviorally, atypical sensory engagement is likely to shape the emergence of motor exploration and self-regulation. Reduced spontaneous activity monitoring in toddlers with ASD is consistent with the possibility that altered levels of environmental sampling and bodily engagement are already evident before or around the time of diagnosis ref [18]. Related work comparing ASD and ADHD indicates partially distinct sensory-motor learning profiles, with autism characterized by over-selective reliance on proprioceptive input, whereas ADHD shows difficulties integrating multiple sensory inputs ref [31]. Although this evidence comes from later developmental periods, it offers a plausible framework for interpreting infant differences in postural control, object exploration, and adaptive attention shifting.

Importantly, sensory atypicalities may also cascade into everyday regulatory domains. Associations between sensory processing abnormalities and eating problems in ASD illustrate how early responsivity differences can affect feeding, arousal, and parent-infant co-regulation ref [34]. In high-risk sibling cohorts, 18-month behavioral predictors already capture variation in later outcomes, indicating that sensorimotor and regulatory signals should be considered alongside social-communicative measures when identifying early developmental divergence ref [7]. Taken together, the literature supports a model in which early sensory and motor features are not peripheral findings, but central organizing dimensions of emerging neurodevelopmental risk.

subsections.section_title: Early Behavioral and Cognitive Markers in Infancy
subsections.subsection_title: Early Behavioral and Cognitive Markers in Infancy - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A particularly informative candidate marker in infancy is atypical attentional control, especially slowed visual disengagement from salient stimuli. Across experimental paradigms, impairments in disengaging attention have been repeatedly linked to autism spectrum disorder and are detectable early in development, suggesting that basic orienting mechanisms may constrain later social learning opportunities and the efficient sampling of complex environments ref [22]. Eye-tracking approaches have therefore become important for quantifying these early differences in attentional allocation and flexibility in infants at elevated likelihood for ASD ref [32].

These attentional differences should not be viewed as isolated deficits, but as part of broader developmental divergence. Work on developmental trajectories in toddlers with ASD indicates that symptom emergence is heterogeneous, with some children showing early and persistent difficulties and others exhibiting more gradual change across domains ref [25]. Within this framework, early problems in disengagement, orienting, and state regulation may be among the processes that help channel infants toward distinct developmental pathways, rather than serving as disorder-specific markers in a simple one-to-one sense ref [25], ref [45].

The practical importance of such early markers lies in their potential to support intervention before consolidated behavioral syndromes are evident. Reviews of the rationale for very early intervention argue that subtle disruptions in attention, social engagement, and reciprocal interaction during the first years may alter the developmental cascade that culminates in later ASD symptoms ref [31]. This perspective is also consistent with broader accounts emphasizing that early-developing cognitive and social mechanisms scaffold later specialization, making infancy a critical period for identifying emerging atypical trajectories and for designing preventive supports ref [16], ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Early Behavioral and Cognitive Markers in Infancy
subsections.subsection_title: Early Behavioral and Cognitive Markers in Infancy - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A further class of early markers concerns infant regulation across affective, physiological, and sensory domains. Although much of the regulation literature in autism has focused on later childhood, systematic review evidence indicates that emotion-regulation differences are pervasive and measurable across multiple levels of analysis, supporting the view that early disturbances in arousal modulation may be developmentally significant ref [24]. In infants at elevated likelihood for ASD, atypical cry acoustics by 6 months provide one concrete example of altered early signal production that may reflect differences in neurobehavioral organization and state regulation rather than social communication alone ref [14].

Sensory responsivity is also relevant to early trajectories because atypical thresholds for orienting, soothing, and environmental adaptation may precede clearer behavioral syndromes. Work on sensory processing in autism has consistently documented unusual patterns of reactivity and modulation, suggesting that sensory atypicalities may be part of the developmental substrate from which later social and behavioral symptoms emerge ref [13]. Complementing behavioral observations, reviews of cardiac autonomic measures highlight the importance of autonomic regulation as an index of physiological flexibility, with altered autonomic responding in ASD offering a plausible mechanism linking sensory over- or under-responsivity to difficulties in attention and self-regulation ref [10].

These regulatory markers are especially important in the context of overlapping ASD–ADHD pathways. Reviews of comorbidity emphasize that attentional dysregulation, impulsive response tendencies, and difficulties modulating behavior are not unique to either condition and may co-occur from early in development ref [9], ref [28]. Thus, early abnormalities in cry, sensory responsivity, and autonomic regulation may be best conceptualized as transdiagnostic indicators of atypical developmental organization, with their later phenotypic expression depending on how regulatory vulnerabilities interact with emerging social, attentional, and motor systems.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches to Prospective Infant Research
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Approaches to Prospective Infant Research - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A core methodological challenge in prospective infant research is how to anchor early behavioral signals to later clinical outcomes. Standardized diagnostic and assessment instruments therefore play a central role, not as stand-alone markers of infant risk, but as outcome-defining tools that permit longitudinal linkage between infancy and later ASD phenotypes. The Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) has been especially influential in this regard because it provides a structured, observational framework for quantifying social-communicative behavior and restricted or repetitive features across development ref [56]. Revisions to ADOS algorithms further improved diagnostic validity, strengthening its utility for harmonizing outcome classification across infant cohort studies ref [6].

At the same time, prospective designs must contend with the limits of diagnosis in very young children. Clinical classification in toddlerhood is feasible, but accuracy depends on developmental level, symptom profile, and the integration of multiple sources of information rather than reliance on any single instrument ref [25], ref [33]. Multisite work has also shown that diagnostic distinctions within the autism spectrum can vary across settings, underscoring the need for standardized procedures and careful attention to inter-clinic reliability when infant studies use later categorical outcomes as validation targets ref [21]. These issues are especially important in high-risk sibling cohorts, where emerging symptoms may be subtle, uneven, and developmentally shifting.

For this reason, the strongest prospective infant studies use diagnostic instruments as one component within a broader assessment architecture that combines repeated behavioral observation, clinician judgment, developmental testing, and dimensional characterization of traits. Such an approach is also compatible with transdiagnostic frameworks, particularly given evidence that some cognitive and neural endophenotypes may cut across ASD and ADHD rather than map neatly onto a single disorder boundary ref [29]. Methodologically, this argues for longitudinal, multi-method phenotyping in which standardized diagnostic tools provide necessary clinical anchors, while dimensional and cross-domain measures capture heterogeneity and developmental change ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches to Prospective Infant Research
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Approaches to Prospective Infant Research - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Prospective infant studies increasingly rely on scalable measurement platforms that bridge laboratory precision with clinically usable screening. Eye-tracking is a prominent example: it can quantify early social attention, orienting, and visual engagement with high temporal resolution, and has been especially valuable for detecting subtle developmental deviations before formal diagnosis is possible. At the same time, its interpretability depends heavily on task design, data quality, and assumptions about what atypical gaze patterns index developmentally, limiting its value as a stand-alone marker ref [12].

Neuroimaging and behavioral phenotyping offer complementary strengths. Structural MRI work showing early brain enlargement and elevated extra-axial fluid in infants later diagnosed with ASD illustrates the promise of biologically proximal markers, but also the practical constraints of cost, motion sensitivity, and limited feasibility for population-scale screening ref [8]. By contrast, parent-report and rating-scale approaches are inexpensive and broadly deployable, yet require careful validation. Evidence that parent-reported ASD diagnoses can be verified within web-based registries supports their utility for large-scale prospective sampling, while studies of Level 2 ASD rating scales underscore that screening accuracy varies substantially across instruments and contexts, reinforcing the need to separate risk enrichment from diagnosis ref [20], ref [31].

A further methodological priority is transdiagnostic measurement. Reaction time variability has been proposed as a candidate phenotype cutting across ASD and ADHD, highlighting how repeated performance-based measures may capture shared liabilities not visible in categorical case-control designs ref [24]. Overall, the field is moving toward multimethod combinations—digital behavior, neuroimaging, caregiver report, and dimensional cognitive markers—to improve sensitivity to developmental change while preserving translational relevance for early identification.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches to Prospective Infant Research
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Approaches to Prospective Infant Research - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central methodological challenge in prospective infant research is how to combine early screening, repeated behavioral characterization, and later outcome validation without conflating risk markers with disorder-specific indicators. Work on screening and diagnostic instrumentation has emphasized that psychometric properties shift across age, context, and purpose, making instrument selection and calibration especially consequential in infant-sibling and community cohorts ref [16]. This argues for designs in which early measures are treated probabilistically and are interpreted alongside longitudinal follow-up rather than as stand-alone proxies for diagnosis.

Longitudinal infant-sibling studies illustrate the value of this approach. In large consortium work, 18-month measures predicted later heterogenous outcomes, but no single marker was determinative, underscoring both the predictive utility and limits of early behavioral phenotyping ref [7]. Similar issues arise for putative neurophysiological biomarkers: developmental change in resting EEG power appears informative as an endophenotypic signal, yet its meaning depends on trajectory, timing, and relation to later phenotype rather than on a single cross-sectional observation ref [12]. Reviews of biomarkers in ASD likewise caution that translational progress depends on replication, developmental sensitivity, and integration across biological and behavioral levels ref [28].

Accordingly, prospective studies are strongest when they use multi-method measurement batteries that bridge overt behavior and mechanistic candidate markers. Even relatively simple tools such as actigraphy or limited activity monitoring can add ecologically relevant information about early motor and regulatory patterns, although these measures also require careful interpretation and standardization ref [18]. Taken together, these methods support a transdiagnostic, developmental strategy: repeated measurement, harmonized phenotyping, and outcome-based validation are more informative than reliance on any single early screen or biomarker ref [16], ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches to Prospective Infant Research
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Approaches to Prospective Infant Research - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A major methodological advance in prospective infant research is the integration of neuroimaging and experimental attention paradigms to characterize mechanisms that precede formal diagnosis. Structural MRI offers a noninvasive route to quantifying early brain growth and regional anatomy, but its translational value depends on careful consideration of developmental timing, motion, and the interpretive limits of heterogeneous case definitions ref [20]. Functional MRI can in principle extend this work to neural systems, yet pediatric feasibility remains a substantial constraint; success rates vary across neurodevelopmental groups, underscoring the practical challenge of obtaining usable data in infants and young children and the consequent risk of biased samples ref [7].

Because of these constraints, many prospective studies pair imaging with lower-burden behavioral assays. Visual disengagement paradigms are particularly informative because they can be administered early, repeated longitudinally, and linked to emerging attentional control differences relevant to both ASD and ADHD pathways; at the same time, the literature shows that disengagement effects are not uniformly specific and must be interpreted within broader developmental profiles ref [22]. This logic aligns with trajectory-based approaches showing that toddlers later diagnosed with ASD do not follow a single developmental course, which argues for repeated measurement rather than reliance on one-time assessments ref [25].

Methodologically, infant-sibling and familial-likelihood designs further strengthen inference by enriching samples for later difficulties while allowing examination of subclinical variation related to the broader autism phenotype ref [19]. Such designs are especially valuable when coupled with developmental monitoring and preventive intervention frameworks, since the rationale for very early intervention depends on detecting risk signals before symptoms consolidate ref [31]. Overall, the field is moving toward multimethod, longitudinal, and transdiagnostic designs that combine feasibility with mechanistic depth.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches to Prospective Infant Research
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Approaches to Prospective Infant Research - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final methodological priority is linking prospective infant markers to clinically usable screening and measurement frameworks. Population-based and pediatric-setting studies show both the promise and limits of early identification: systematic screening can detect elevated likelihood in the second year of life, but accuracy depends on developmental timing, referral pathways, and the balance between sensitivity and specificity in general-population settings ref [18], ref [27]. These studies are especially important for translation because infant-risk cohorts, while powerful for mechanism, do not by themselves establish performance in routine services.

Measurement choices also shape inference. Reviews of diagnostic and rating instruments emphasize that reliability and validity cannot be assumed when tools are extended downward in age or across contexts; instrument performance must be evaluated for its intended purpose, whether screening, case confirmation, or dimensional characterization ref [30]. This is particularly relevant for prospective work seeking transdiagnostic profiles spanning ASD and ADHD, given longstanding overlap in attentional, regulatory, and behavioral features across the two conditions ref [28].

Accordingly, scalable prospective designs increasingly benefit from combining brief behavioral screening with low-burden quantitative markers and dimensional outcome measures. Candidate additions include cry acoustics in early infancy, which may capture subtle atypicality before overt symptoms consolidate ref [14], autonomic indices that index arousal and regulation but require careful standardization of acquisition and interpretation ref [10], and broader emotion-regulation measures, where current reviews highlight substantial heterogeneity and limited consensus on optimal operationalization ref [24]. Together, these considerations argue for multi-method, longitudinal, and transdiagnostic measurement strategies that are psychometrically robust and feasible for real-world early detection.

subsections.section_title: Developmental Outcomes, Comorbidity, and Functional Consequences
subsections.subsection_title: Developmental Outcomes, Comorbidity, and Functional Consequences - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Early atypical developmental pathways in autism are clinically significant not only because they predict core social-communication and behavioral features, but also because they are linked to a broad burden of co-occurring conditions that shape long-term outcome. Intellectual disability remains a major source of heterogeneity in autism, influencing language, learning, adaptive skill acquisition, and the intensity of support required across development ref [66]. Beyond cognition, childhood autism is frequently accompanied by additional psychiatric symptoms, indicating that later impairment often reflects more than autism severity alone ref [20].

Among these comorbidities, anxiety is especially prominent and can substantially worsen social participation, behavioral regulation, and family functioning in children and adolescents with autism ref [64]. Overlap with ADHD is likewise common, with co-occurrence associated with greater behavioral dysregulation and more complex clinical presentation than either condition alone ref [31]. Autism is also associated with elevated rates of sleep disturbance and gastrointestinal problems, both of which may exacerbate irritability, inattention, and everyday functional difficulties while adding to caregiver burden ref [12], ref [11].

These developmental and medical-psychiatric burdens persist into later life. Even adults with average intelligence often experience substantial psychiatric symptoms and psychosocial difficulties, demonstrating that ostensibly preserved intellectual ability does not guarantee adaptive success ref [67]. In adulthood, functional consequences are particularly evident in employment, where social demands, executive difficulties, and limited workplace supports contribute to underemployment and instability ref [19]. Taken together, infant and early-childhood neurodevelopmental differences should be understood as the starting point of a lifespan trajectory marked by multidomain comorbidity and uneven functional outcomes.

subsections.section_title: Developmental Outcomes, Comorbidity, and Functional Consequences
subsections.subsection_title: Developmental Outcomes, Comorbidity, and Functional Consequences - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A striking feature of later developmental outcome in autism is the high burden of additional psychiatric disorder. Structured diagnostic assessment has shown that children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder frequently meet criteria for multiple DSM-defined conditions, indicating that core social-communication difficulties rarely occur in isolation ref [30]. This comorbidity has important developmental implications because it compounds symptom severity, complicates clinical presentation, and contributes to more variable trajectories from childhood into adolescence.

Adolescence appears to be a particularly sensitive period in which difficulties in emotion regulation may intensify functional risk. Compared with typically developing peers, adolescents with high-functioning autism show atypical emotion regulation patterns, and these disturbances are associated with greater psychiatric symptomatology ref [34]. Such findings suggest that emerging internalizing and behavioral problems are not merely epiphenomena but may reflect downstream consequences of earlier neurodevelopmental differences interacting with increasing social and self-regulatory demands.

The functional consequences extend beyond the individual to the family context. As autistic individuals and those with ADHD move into adolescence and adulthood, caregivers report substantial and persistent burden, highlighting that long-term outcome should be evaluated in relational and ecological as well as symptom-based terms ref [23]. Taken together, evidence on psychiatric comorbidity, emotion regulation difficulties, and caregiver burden underscores that early atypical pathways are linked to broad psychosocial consequences across development rather than to diagnostic status alone ref [23], ref [30], ref [34].

subsections.section_title: Developmental Outcomes, Comorbidity, and Functional Consequences
subsections.subsection_title: Developmental Outcomes, Comorbidity, and Functional Consequences - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Beyond core diagnostic symptoms, later functional consequences of autism frequently extend into the family and social ecology surrounding the child. Service use and associated financial demands can be substantial, with early evidence indicating measurable impacts on parental time, formal support needs, and household costs, underscoring that developmental divergence in infancy may have enduring consequences well beyond the individual child ref [71]. These burdens are not uniformly absorbed, but interact with caregiving demands and the severity of associated behavioural features, including co-occurring ADHD symptoms, which are linked to greater behavioural phenotype severity in autistic children ref [19].

Social functioning is another major downstream domain. A systematic review of friendship in children with autism highlights persistent difficulties in forming, maintaining, and reciprocally navigating peer relationships, even when children express interest in social connection ref [74]. Such peer impairments are clinically important because they shape participation, school adjustment, and vulnerability to later psychosocial difficulties. In parallel, family studies show that caring for a child with autism is associated with reduced parental quality of life, reflecting strains across emotional, practical, and relational domains ref [27].

These effects can accumulate at the broader family level. Population-based work suggests elevated relationship strain among parents of children with autism ref [30], while qualitative evidence from low-resource settings documents substantial unmet needs, coping challenges, and gaps in service access for families raising an autistic child ref [11]. Taken together, the literature indicates that early atypical developmental pathways are associated with a wide spectrum of later consequences, spanning comorbid behavioural difficulties, friendship and participation challenges, and significant family-level psychosocial and economic burden ref [71], ref [74], ref [11], ref [27], ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Developmental Outcomes, Comorbidity, and Functional Consequences
subsections.subsection_title: Developmental Outcomes, Comorbidity, and Functional Consequences - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Beyond core symptom expression, autism is associated with substantial functional consequences across everyday life domains. Adaptive behavior difficulties often exceed what would be expected from cognitive level alone, and these impairments can persist into adulthood, including marked limitations in independent living skills among individuals with more severe intellectual disability and autism ref [17]. Sleep disturbance further compounds outcome variability, being linked to poorer cognitive performance and weaker adaptive functioning, suggesting that associated health problems may amplify developmental burden over time ref [78].

Psychiatric comorbidity also broadens the clinical significance of early atypical developmental pathways. Reviews have highlighted elevated rates of anxiety, affective disturbance, and psychosis-related phenomena in autistic populations, underscoring that later outcome cannot be understood solely in terms of social-communication symptoms and repetitive behavior ref [9]. Social participation is additionally compromised by adverse peer experiences: youth with autism are at heightened risk of bullying victimization relative to comparison groups, with likely downstream effects on emotional adjustment, school engagement, and self-concept ref [11]. Consistent with this wider framing, critical review evidence indicates that quality of life in autistic children and adolescents is shaped by social, emotional, and contextual factors rather than symptom severity alone ref [28].

Functional consequences also extend beyond the individual child to the family system. Siblings may show distinctive social, emotional, and behavioral adjustment challenges, although findings are heterogeneous and moderated by family context ref [83]. Parents report both substantial stress and burden, as well as experiences of adaptation and personal growth, indicating that family outcomes are multidimensional rather than uniformly negative ref [23]. Qualitative work with mothers similarly emphasizes pervasive impacts on family routines, relationships, and future planning ref [24]. Together, these findings reinforce that early neurodevelopmental divergence has long-range implications for mental health, participation, and family functioning.

subsections.section_title: Developmental Outcomes, Comorbidity, and Functional Consequences
subsections.subsection_title: Developmental Outcomes, Comorbidity, and Functional Consequences - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Beyond childhood symptom expression, early atypical developmental pathways have consequences for participation across the life course. Reviews of community and school participation indicate that autistic children and ახალგაზრდents often show restricted engagement in social, recreational, and community contexts, with barriers arising not only from core social-communication differences but also from environmental demands and limited supports ref [33]. In educational settings, victimization is a particularly important downstream consequence, with elevated rates of bullying and peer victimization linked to social vulnerability, communication difficulties, and mainstream placement without adequate support ref [26].

Clinical comorbidity further amplifies functional burden. Co-occurring ADHD is common in autism and is associated with greater impairment in attention, self-regulation, and everyday functioning than either condition alone, complicating both assessment and intervention planning ref [9]. Similarly, disruptive behavior disorders and externalizing symptoms can substantially interfere with schooling, family functioning, and access to community activities ref [89]. Although combined treatment approaches are increasingly discussed, the evidence base for managing co-occurring ADHD and ASD remains more limited than clinical need would suggest, underscoring the importance of longitudinal, developmentally informed care ref [12].

Later outcomes also highlight the persistence of functional challenges into adulthood and old age. Systematic review evidence suggests that work participation in autistic adults is shaped by cognitive ability, social and communicative competence, educational history, comorbid mental health problems, and the availability of workplace accommodations and support services ref [87]. At the same time, ageing in autistic people remains understudied, with emerging work pointing to continuing needs in mental health, daily living support, and social inclusion across adulthood ref [29]. These broader functional sequelae extend to families as well, as both mothers and fathers report substantial and evolving support needs when raising autistic children and adolescents ref [21].

subsections.section_title: Implications for Early Identification, Intervention, and Future Research
subsections.subsection_title: Implications for Early Identification, Intervention, and Future Research - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A central implication of the infant literature is that early identification should move away from a late, single-threshold diagnostic model toward repeated developmental surveillance that is sensitive to both autism-specific and cross-disorder risk. Reviews of age at ASD diagnosis show substantial delays and variability attributable to child characteristics, family factors, and service systems, indicating that opportunities for earlier recognition are often missed rather than biologically unavailable ref [14]. At the same time, evidence-based assessment frameworks emphasize that screening and diagnostic decisions are most robust when they integrate parent report, direct observation, and developmental history, rather than relying on any single marker or instrument ref [33]. For very young children, diagnostic practice reviews further suggest that clinically meaningful ASD identification is feasible by 2 to 3 years when assessment is developmentally informed and longitudinally anchored ref [25].

These points are especially important in infants showing mixed or nonspecific early difficulties, because ASD and ADHD are not fully separable at the level of liability. Shared heritability findings support the view that early attentional, regulatory, and social atypicalities may index partly overlapping neurodevelopmental risk rather than discrete pathways from the outset ref [17]. Related reviews of common cognitive and brain endophenotypes, together with work on ASD–ADHD co-occurrence, reinforce the need for transdiagnostic monitoring strategies that track emerging profiles over time instead of forcing premature categorical decisions ref [29], ref [31].

For intervention, the practical corollary is to act on early developmental concern even when diagnostic certainty is incomplete. Systematic review evidence indicates that parent-implemented early intervention can improve proximal child outcomes and caregiver interactional strategies, making it well suited to the prediagnostic or prodromal period ref [15]. Future research should therefore test staged models in which repeated early assessment is directly linked to low-burden, developmentally targeted support, while also examining whether infant markers can differentiate pathways to ASD, ADHD, and their overlap with sufficient precision to guide personalized intervention timing and content ref [15], ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Implications for Early Identification, Intervention, and Future Research
subsections.subsection_title: Implications for Early Identification, Intervention, and Future Research - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A key implication for early identification is the need to move beyond single-behavior screening toward developmentally layered risk assessment. Evidence from Level 2 autism rating scales indicates that screening performance is variable and strongly shaped by age, symptom profile, and referral context, underscoring the limits of relying on one instrument at one time point ref [31]. More comprehensive early-detection models should therefore combine parent-report and clinical observation with objective markers that can capture emerging atypicality before behavioral symptoms fully consolidate ref [17], ref [31].

Several candidate markers are especially relevant in this respect. Eye-tracking approaches offer scalable indices of visual attention and social orienting, although their translational value depends on standardization, test-retest reliability, and demonstration of incremental validity over existing behavioral tools ref [12]. Likewise, early brain enlargement and elevated extra-axial fluid suggest that neurobiological signatures may help identify a subgroup of infants on an autism pathway before diagnosis is clinically secure, but these findings currently support stratification research more than routine screening ref [8]. Together, these data argue for multimethod risk algorithms rather than biomarker exceptionalism.

Future work should also incorporate trans-diagnostic indicators that may cut across ASD and ADHD. Reaction time variability is one such candidate phenotype, with potential relevance for identifying infants whose later difficulties involve attentional control rather than, or in addition to, social-communication impairment ref [24]. This has direct intervention implications: early monitoring systems should be designed to detect divergence in multiple developmental domains, so that supports can be tailored to emerging profiles rather than to a single categorical endpoint ref [17]. Priority research questions include when multimodal markers add clinically meaningful prediction, how they generalize across settings, and whether they improve timing and targeting of preventive intervention ref [8], ref [12], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Implications for Early Identification, Intervention, and Future Research
subsections.subsection_title: Implications for Early Identification, Intervention, and Future Research - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central implication for early identification is that prediction should move from single markers toward developmental profiling that integrates behavior, physiology, and context. Work in infant siblings shows that 18-month signs have value for forecasting later outcome, but also that prediction is probabilistic and heterogeneous rather than deterministic ref [18]. This argues against one-time screening models and supports repeated surveillance using measures calibrated to developmental change. At the same time, longstanding measurement problems in autism screening and diagnosis caution that instruments optimized for categorical case finding may be less sensitive to subthreshold, evolving, or mixed ASD–ADHD presentations in infancy ref [16].

Relatedly, biomarker research is most useful when embedded in clinically interpretable models. Reviews of autism biomarkers emphasize both promise and limited translational readiness, suggesting that candidate markers should be evaluated for incremental validity beyond behavioral assessment rather than treated as stand-alone diagnostic tools ref [28]. Resting EEG trajectories illustrate this point: neural measures may capture atypical developmental pathways before full clinical consolidation, but they require longitudinal replication and linkage to functional outcomes to become actionable in practice ref [12]. Future work should therefore prioritize multimodal prediction frameworks that test whether physiological signals improve timing, specificity, and developmental targeting of referral decisions.

Intervention research also points toward stratified, mechanism-informed care. Treatment individualization frameworks argue that heterogeneity should guide the matching of intervention content and intensity to child characteristics, rather than assuming uniform response across young children with autism ref [25]. Sensory-based phenotypes may offer one route to such stratification ref [29], especially given evidence that sensory-motor learning differs across ASD and ADHD, with autism showing greater reliance on proprioceptive input and ADHD depending more on integrated multisensory information ref [31]. A key future priority is to determine whether these early phenotypic distinctions can prospectively inform personalized preventive interventions for infants showing emerging social, attentional, or regulatory risk.

subsections.section_title: Implications for Early Identification, Intervention, and Future Research
subsections.subsection_title: Implications for Early Identification, Intervention, and Future Research - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central implication for future research is the need to move beyond single early markers toward developmental risk models that integrate familial liability, early cognitive-attentional traits, and evolving symptom trajectories. Work on the broader autism phenotype suggests that subclinical familial traits may index inherited liability long before categorical diagnosis is possible, supporting family-informed surveillance strategies rather than reliance on later behavioral thresholds alone [19]. This view is also consistent with evidence that autism severity reflects both de novo and familial influences, underscoring the importance of models that accommodate multiple developmental pathways to similar clinical outcomes [34].

Such models should be explicitly dynamic. Reviews of visual disengagement indicate that attentional control differences are detectable across development and may represent one candidate process for stratifying infants at elevated likelihood, although not all infants who later develop ASD show the same profile [22]. Likewise, longitudinal work on toddlers with ASD demonstrates heterogeneous developmental trajectories rather than a uniform course, implying that early identification systems must be sensitive to timing, slope, and pattern of change, not simply symptom presence at one age [25].

These considerations have direct intervention implications. Arguments for very early intervention in high-risk infants emphasize acting during periods of heightened neurodevelopmental plasticity, before maladaptive patterns consolidate [31]. At the same time, naturalistic outcome data from preschool intervention cohorts indicate substantial variability in response, reinforcing the need for individualized and developmentally staged treatment planning [26]. Future studies should therefore link prediagnostic markers, familial context, and trajectory-based phenotypes to treatment response, with the goal of matching infants and toddlers to the right intervention targets at the right developmental moment.

subsections.section_title: Implications for Early Identification, Intervention, and Future Research
subsections.subsection_title: Implications for Early Identification, Intervention, and Future Research - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final implication is that future early-identification frameworks should move beyond single-disorder case finding and instead adopt developmental surveillance models sensitive to overlap between ASD and ADHD. Reviews of their comorbidity consistently indicate that the two conditions co-occur at rates too high to be treated as incidental, with partially shared phenotypic liabilities that can obscure early differential recognition if screening is narrowly autism-specific or ADHD-specific ref [9], ref [28]. This argues for infant and toddler monitoring strategies that track social communication, attentional control, activity regulation, and emerging behavioral flexibility in parallel.

Population screening studies further suggest both the promise and the limits of very early detection. Systematic pediatric screening can increase case ascertainment and reduce reliance on passive referral pathways, supporting a public-health approach to earlier recognition ref [18]. At the same time, evidence that some children with ASD can be identified at 18 months in general population samples highlights feasibility, but also implies that sensitivity at this age is imperfect and that repeated screening across development is likely necessary ref [27]. For children showing mixed early features, staged surveillance may be especially important, because early social-communication concerns may later be accompanied by clearer attentional or hyperactive symptoms.

Intervention research should therefore prioritize transdiagnostic and adaptive models for infants and toddlers on neurodevelopmental risk pathways. Clinical work on co-occurring ASD and ADHD indicates that treatment planning must anticipate combined impairments rather than addressing each condition in isolation ref [12]. A key research priority is to test whether earlier support for regulation, parent-child interaction, and environmental scaffolding can alter developmental cascades before categorical diagnoses fully consolidate, while also determining which early profiles forecast ASD, ADHD, or persistent co-occurring presentations ref [9], ref [12], ref [28].
